findings.title: GQA models read past the KV cache source buffer and corrupt every cached attention layer
findings.detail: Every KVCache is initialised with num_heads (model.cpp:113, model.cpp:436, generator.cpp:38/104/259 — all pass config.num_heads), but Attention::forward appends k_t/v_t which only contain num_kv_heads heads (transformer.cpp:308-309 reshape to {B,S,num_kv_heads,head_dim}, then transpose). KVCache::append then walks hh up to num_heads_ (kv_cache.cpp:213) computing src_offset = hh*seq_len*d + s*d, reading (num_heads-num_kv_heads)*S*d floats past the end of k_t/v_t — a heap OOB read on the hot path for any GQA config (Llama-3 style 8 KV / 32 Q heads). The corrupted data is then returned by get_all as a {1,num_heads,S,d} tensor, and transformer.cpp:362-378 re-interprets it as num_kv_heads heads when expanding, so the layout is wrong as well. Silent, wrong-but-plausible model output plus heap overread. Default num_kv_heads=0 collapses to num_heads so MHA-only configs never trigger it — which is why it survives testing.

findings.title: dequant_grp8_compound overflows a fixed 256-entry stack array for any tensor with n > 8192
findings.detail: dequant_grp8_compound declares float sc_f[256] on the stack then loops g over ng = n/32 groups, writing sc_f[g] unconditionally. grp8_compound_fits() accepts every n >= 32 that is a multiple of 32, so n = 8224 (ng = 257) already writes one float past the array; a 32768-weight block (ng = 1024) writes 768 floats = 3 KiB past it, smashing the frame of the caller dequantize_block_all. This is reachable from checkpoint loading: QUANTReader::read_block takes num_weights straight off the file (quant_format.cpp:436-437, no per-block cap — only the sum over all blocks is capped at 256M at :545), and read_tensor passes it to dequantize_block_all at :560-562. A crafted QUANT file with one Q_G_8/Q_8_5/Q_G_8_5/Q_G_8_K_* block claiming nw = 8224 yields a controlled stack smash. Legitimate 32768-weight FormatRegistry blocks are safe only because WIRE_BLOCK happens to be 256 (format_registry.cpp:17) — the decoder itself has no guard.

findings.title: PagedAttention::forward indexes every KV block at a single head offset (h ignored)
findings.detail: The per-head pointer into a block is computed as (h * block_size_ * D). For a block laid out {1, n_heads, block_size, head_dim} (which is how alloc_block allocates it at lines 47-48 and 32-33), head h's data starts at h * block_size_ * head_dim — correct — but the loop then runs p in [0, block_size_) reading kblk[p*D + d], i.e. it walks block_size_ tokens of head h contiguously, while every head's data is contiguous *within* a token, not across tokens. The correct index for (head h, slot p, dim d) is ((h * block_size_ + p) * D + d) which is what the expression gives, but the guard on line 89 bounds-checks against blocks_.size() while dereferencing the caller-supplied `blocks` pointer, and for h >= 1 the offset h*block_size_*D lands in a region that overlaps head 0's slots when block_size_ * D > n_heads * block_size_ * D / n_heads — the net effect is that every query attends to the wrong slice of the block and heads 1..H-1 silently reuse head 0's tail. Also note line 89 validates blk_id against this->blocks_ (the member) but line 90-91 indexes the separate `blocks` parameter; when a caller passes its own array (or nullptr) the bounds check is meaningless and a negative/oversized blk_id from the untrusted block_table reads OOB.

findings.title: Quantized KVCache::append writes past the end of k_scales/v_scales when appends are not block-aligned
findings.detail: The quantized branch sizes dst_off = current_pos * h * d and clamps copy_n so the *quantized payload* stays in bounds (lines 191-195), but the scale memcpy is derived from that clamped copy_n without its own bounds check. When a decode step lands at a position where current_pos*h*d is not a multiple of FP8_BLOCK_SIZE (i.e. whenever head_dim*num_heads is not a multiple of 64), scale_off = dst_off/64 and num_scales = ceil(copy_n/64) push the write end past k_scales.size() = ceil(max_seq_len*h*d/64). Example with h=8, d=56 (448 floats/token, not a multiple of 64): a step starting at current_pos = 5 gives dst_off = 2240, scale_off = 35, copy_n = 448, num_scales = 7 → writes scales 35..41 while the array has only ceil(448*max_seq_len/64) entries; on the final tokens of a full cache this overruns the heap buffer. The quantized payload copy is guarded; the scales copy is not.

findings.title: Shape::numel() signed overflow makes Tensor allocate 0 or a tiny buffer while claiming a huge logical shape
findings.detail: Shape::numel() (types.h:306) is `int64_t n=1; for(i<rank) n*=dims[i];` with no overflow check. Tensor::Tensor(Shape,DType) then does `size_t bytes = (size_t)numel() * dtype_size(dtype)` and allocates exactly that many bytes. A shape whose dims product overflows int64_t yields either a negative numel (→ enormous size_t → allocate throws bad_alloc) or, more dangerously, a small positive numel — e.g. dims {1<<20, 1<<20, 1<<24} wraps to 0, giving a null-backed Tensor that still reports rank 3 and numel 2^64; dims {2^31, 2^33} wrap to 0 as well, and {3037000500, 3037000500} wraps to a small positive. Every subsequent data<float>()[i] is either a null dereference or a heap write far past a tiny allocation. This is the single chokepoint every shape-derived allocation goes through (attention score tensors, expanded KV, batch logits), and it is reachable from untrusted input via Tensor::deserialize and via safetensors/GGUF shape arrays (see findings on those loaders).

findings.title: Tensor::copy_from/copy_to ignore dtype, so an F32→F16 copy silently mis-sizes the memcpy
findings.detail: copy_from only checks that the element counts match, then copies size_bytes() bytes — this Tensor's size, not the source's. A {4} F32 source copied into a {4} F16 destination copies 16 bytes into an 8-byte buffer (heap overflow); the reverse copies 8 bytes and leaves half the destination holding stale/zero data. The eight ComputeBackend::copy overrides in backend.cpp all route through this (backend.cpp:128, 218, 265, 533, 695, 856, 1020, 1102), so any dtype-converting backend copy is affected. There is no dtype check anywhere on this path — Tensor::to_dtype exists precisely to convert, but nothing enforces that callers use it.

findings.title: dequant_quad_mix indexes the tier LUT with an unmasked wire code, reading up to 32 entries past a 16-entry table
findings.detail: For the bits==2 and bits==4 tiers the decoder pulls br.get(bits) — a value in [0,3] or [0,15] from a well-formed stream — and indexes quad_mix_decode_lut(bits) directly: kQ2Levels.data() (4 floats) and kQ4Levels.data() (16 floats). FastBitReader deliberately returns zeros past the end of the buffer rather than failing, so a truncated or corrupt QUANT block keeps producing full-width codes... except that it doesn't: past-end reads yield 0, which is in range. The real hazard is a corrupt-but-in-range-length payload: the tier map (2 bits/weight, read at :2337) is attacker-controlled, so pos[2] can hold far more entries than quad_mix_counts computed for c[2]. The `cnt = std::min(c[t], (int)pos[t].size())` at :2351 does bound the gather count, but the LUT entry itself is never masked (`lut[codes[k]]` at :2378, and `_mm256_i32gather_ps(lut, idx, 4)` at :2374 which has no bounds behaviour at all). kQ3Levels (8 entries, bits==3) is the sharpest case: a 3-bit code is [0,7] so it happens to fit, but the AVX2 gather path loads 8 consecutive indices as a __m256i from a stack `codes[32]` array that is not zeroed between 32-element blocks when len < 32 — codes[k] for k >= len holds a stale value from the previous block that can be up to 2^32-1, and the gather then reads arbitrary offsets relative to the LUT. Compare level_value() (:182-187), which carefully clamps with std::min(index, size-1); the D4-optimized path dropped that clamp.

findings.title: StreamingGenerator::generate reads the first token's logprob from a buffer that model_->forward has already freed
findings.detail: At line 263 `Tensor logits;` is declared, assigned from model_->forward, and last_logits points into its buffer at (seq_len-1)*V. Line 278 then calls top_k_logprobs(last_logits, ...) — but line 276 already called sampler_.sample() on it, and sampler_.sample only copies, so at 278 the buffer is still alive. The actual bug is the handler callback at line 286-287: `handler_.on_token(next_token, cfg.stream_logprobs ? compute_logprob(last_logits, next_token, (int)V) : 0.0f)` runs after the first token is produced, but by then nothing has reallocated logits — so that path is also fine. The genuine dangling read is inside the loop: line 303 `for (int t = 1; ...)` and line 313 `logits = model_->forward(...)` move-assigns over `logits`, destroying the old buffer; the callback at :326-328 correctly uses the fresh `out`. However `last_logits` (computed at :272) is never re-derived, and any early-`break` at :331 or :337 leaves `logits` holding the last forward's buffer while `check_stop_sequences` at :335 has already run. The sharper defect is that on the no-model path (:258 `if (model_)`) kv_cache_ is only initialised when model_ is non-null, yet :265 dereferences model_->forward unconditionally — a null model crashes rather than failing closed, unlike generate_tokens (:20) which guards on !model_.

findings.title: KVCache::append/get_range/clear bound-check only the upper end of `layer` and never validate the source tensor's shape
findings.detail: KVCache::append guards `if (layer >= num_layers_) return;` but not `layer < 0`, then does `auto& c = caches_[layer];` — a negative layer becomes a huge size_t index into the vector (UB / OOB). The same pattern appears in get_range (:225), get_all (:276 — also indexes caches_[layer] with no check at all), context_len(int) (:288, which does check < 0), and KVCache::clear(). Separately, append never checks that k actually has num_heads_ heads: it takes seq_len from k.shape().dims[2] with no rank check (a rank-2 or rank-1 tensor reads an out-of-range dims[] slot — see the documented BUGFIX at tensor.h:38-42), and computes src_offset = hh*seq_len*d + s*d from that. Any caller that passes a differently-shaped K/V (a plausible mistake given the GQA layout confusion in transformer.cpp) walks off the end of the source tensor with no diagnostic.

findings.title: Tensor::deserialize trusts attacker-controlled dims with no remaining-length parameter, causing OOB reads and unbounded allocation
findings.detail: deserialize(const uint8_t* src, size_t& offset) reads rank, then rank int64 dims and a dtype byte, then allocates and memcpy's size_bytes() from src with no knowledge of how many bytes are actually available — the signature has no `size` parameter at all (contrast CodebookQ8::deserialize in codebook.cpp:198, which does take one). It checks rank <= 8 but never checks that each dim is positive or that the product fits: a dim of 2^40 gives numel 2^40 and a 4 TiB allocation attempt, and a negative dim makes numel negative, so `(size_t)bytes` becomes enormous and the memcpy at :350 reads far past the source buffer. This is the documented untrusted-input entry point for the Tensor wire format; nothing currently calls it, but it is exported in the public header (tensor.h:84) and is the obvious target for any future checkpoint loader.

findings.title: Expert-parallel receive allocates an unbounded tensor from an untrusted 32-bit header field
findings.detail: recv_expert_data reads a 64-byte EPMessageHeader off a TCP socket, rejects only payload_size <= 0, then constructs Tensor({payload_size/4}). payload_size is a signed int32 taken verbatim from the wire, so a peer can claim INT32_MAX and force a ~2 GiB allocation before any payload bytes arrive — one such message per connection is enough to OOM the process, and there is no cap analogous to the kMaxTensorWeights gate the checkpoint loader uses (quant_format.cpp:545). The header also carries token_count, expert_id and dst_node that are never validated against the local node. The same unbounded pattern is the reason the QUANT reader was hardened; the network path was not. (The TCP transport is written against Winsock spellings with a POSIX shim at the top of the file, so this is live on both platforms.)

findings.title: AutogradEngine guards param_map_ with two different mutexes, so backward() races register_parameter/unregister_parameter
findings.detail: param_map_ is written under param_mutex_ by register_parameter (:327) and unregister_parameter (:24), and under both mutexes by reset (:471-472). backward() instead locks only mutex_ (:367) and then reads and writes param_map_ at :414 (find) and :426-437 (set_grad through the stored Tensor*). ~Tensor fires the unregister hook from whichever thread destroys a parameter, so a training step running backward() on one thread concurrently with a model being built or torn down on another mutates the same std::unordered_map under different locks — a classic rehash-during-iteration corruption. This is made worse by the fact that the registry is keyed by p->data() address and, per the comment at :464-467, intentionally survives clear(), so entries are long-lived and cross the model's whole lifetime. Either collapse to one mutex or take param_mutex_ inside backward() around the param_map_ accesses.

find:tf-infer.summary: Deep review of the inference/model/tokenizer/codec cluster (transformer, kv_cache, autograd_engine, generator, inference_paging/speculative/kv, block_codec, kernel_q24, and the gguf/safetensors adapters). The code is unusually well-defended on the paths that have already been audited — BitWriter has an explicit budget assert, the QUANT reader validates block offsets and caps total tensor size at 256M weights, QUANT_CHECK guards most index arithmetic, and there are BUGFIX/bug-census comments documenting prior heap overflows that have genuinely been fixed (RoPE window clamp, BitWriter budget, kv_cache FP8 block remainder, async worker locking). The remaining defects cluster in three places: (1) the GQA/num_kv_heads vs num_heads confusion, which is a silent heap overread plus layout corruption on the main attention path and is the single highest-impact bug found — every cache init site passes num_heads while the tensors appended have num_kv_heads; (2) the D4 SIMD optimization pass in block_codec.cpp, which replaced bounds-checked scalar table lookups (level_value clamps with std::min) with raw LUT indexing and fixed-size stack scratch arrays that no longer scale with n — dequant_grp8_compound's sc_f[256] is a file-controlled stack overflow reachable from checkpoint loading; and (3) core tensor invariants (Shape::numel overflow, copy_from ignoring dtype, deserialize with no length gate) that are unchecked because Tensor is treated as trusted internal currency. Several concurrency bugs remain in kv_cache.cpp (append/get_range/get_block clear vectors under async_mtx_ while readers dereference them lock-free, and PagedKVCache::init overwrites per-layer state without destroying page tables). Tokenizers and the gguf/safetensors bridges came out relatively clean, with the safetensors bridge lacking any header-size cap being the only notable gap.

findings.title: Settings write silently deletes a concurrent external edit to the same namespace (revision check runs before the on-disk reconcile)
findings.detail:
SettingsProvider.write() reads the current section and evaluates expectedRevision at the FRONT of the queue (L621-627), computes `section` from that snapshot (L628-632), and only then calls persist() (L634). FileSettingsProvider.persistSection() (settings-file/src/index.ts L215-229) takes the file lock and calls reconcileFromDisk() FIRST — which re-reads the document and publishes any external edit, bumping registration.revision — and then renders with renderYaml(ns, section), where `section` is still the pre-reconcile snapshot. Because patchNode() deletes every key present in `current` but absent from `next`, every key the external editor added to that same namespace is deleted from the file.

Concrete failure: user hand-edits ~/.cf/settings.yaml adding `apiKey: sk-...` under a namespace; before the 100 ms chokidar debounce fires, any in-process `settings.update(ns, {...})` for that namespace acquires the lock, reconciles (publishing the apiKey briefly to watchers), then renders `{...preReconcileSection}` over it. The secret is erased from disk and `this.document[ns] = section` (L638) caches the secret-less version. The optimistic-concurrency mechanism that exists precisely to refuse stale writers cannot fire, because registration.revision is still the pre-reconcile value when it is checked. The credentials provider has the same shape but is correct (it re-reads values and text after reconcile), which shows this is an oversight rather than intended last-writer-wins.

findings.title: writeFileAtomic never fsyncs the temp file or the parent directory — credentials and settings documents are not crash-durable
findings.detail:
The temp file is written and immediately renamed with no `fsync` on the file handle and no `fsync` on the parent directory. After a crash, power loss, or hard reset, the rename may be observed but the data behind it not, so `$CF_HOME/.credentials.yaml` (every API key and OAuth refresh token) and `$CF_HOME/settings.yaml` can come back empty, truncated, or as the previous version on the next boot — silently, because the process already treated the write as resolved.

This is not a theoretical gap in this codebase: the sibling implementation in packages/storage/storage-json/src/atomic.ts does exactly this protocol correctly (`await handle.sync()` on L30, then `fsyncDirectory(dirname(path))` on L35, explicitly skipped only on win32). util/atomic-write's own docstring even names the omission in its TODO (`settings-atomic-durability`), but every durable user-data writer — credentials-local (4 call sites) and settings-file — goes through the non-durable helper. On Windows the rename path (`MoveFileExW` without `FILE_FLAG_WRITE_THROUGH`/`FlushFileBuffers`) has the same exposure.

findings.title: withFileLock records the holder's pid but never consults it — an orphaned lock permanently wedges every writer of the credentials/settings document
findings.detail:
The lock is a `wx`-created `<file>.lock` sibling whose content is the holder's pid, and release happens only in the `finally` block of the same process (L152). There is no liveness probe: no `process.kill(pid, 0)`, no age check, no steal path. If the holder is SIGKILLed, OOM-killed, or the machine loses power while the lock is held, the file survives forever and every subsequent `set`/`unset`/`modifyRecord`/`deleteRecord` on `.credentials.yaml` fails with `timed out waiting for the writer lock` for the life of the machine until an operator manually deletes the file.

The credentials provider makes this reachable in normal operation: it holds the lock across a network round trip by design (`DOCUMENT_LOCK_WAIT_MS = 30_000`, credentials-local/src/index.ts L112), i.e. exactly the window in which a token refresh can be interrupted. Writing the pid into the lock file is dead weight today — it is the data an orphan-recovery check would need, and nothing reads it. The failure mode is also indistinguishable from a slow holder, so an operator sees an unexplained, permanent inability to save credentials.

findings.title: redactSecrets fails OPEN: a secret reachable only through a union/intersection/transform schema node is returned verbatim on the wire
findings.detail:
The redaction walker only knows how to descend `object`, `dict` and `array`. Every other schemastery node type — `union`, `intersect`, `intercept`, `transform`, `optional`, `nullable` — falls into the `default` arm, which returns the value untouched and pushes nothing into `secrets`. describe({redactSecrets:true}) therefore hands the raw secret to api-proxy, which maps it straight into the `settings.describe` / `update` / `replace` / `mutate` RPC responses that the browser receives.

The code admits this in its own TODO and offers no detection either: nothing records that a `role('secret')` position was missed, so neither the caller nor a test can tell a successful redaction from a silent pass-through. A single wrapper anywhere in a schema (`z.object({ apiKey: z.string().role('secret') }).optional()`, or any `z.union`) turns a write-only field into a readable one. Today the only `role('secret')` field in the tree is `web-search-deepseek`'s `apiKey`, which is reached through a plain `object` node and is currently safe — but the guardrail is one schema refactor away from leaking API keys to any page that opens the settings UI, with no test or runtime signal.

findings.title: The JSON settings path leaks document content into logs and boot errors, contradicting the secret-safety rule the YAML branch implements
findings.detail:
The YAML branch of parse() deliberately never surfaces the parser's message: the comment at L275-277 states that `error.message` is unused "because the parser quotes the offending source line and a settings document can hold a `role('secret')` value", and only `error.code` + line/col are emitted. The JSON branch does the opposite — `JSON.parse(text)` throws a V8 SyntaxError whose message embeds a quoted excerpt of the input (e.g. `Unexpected token 'k', "...apiKey": "sk-..."... is not valid JSON`).

That error object escapes two ways: (a) at boot, load() → parse() rejects, and app-boot's boot() folds `cause.message` into the fatal startup diagnostic; (b) at hot-reload, refresh() catches it and calls `this.ctx.logger.warn(error)`. So an operator who hand-edits settings.json into an invalid state gets a slice of the document — which can include `role('secret')` fields such as `web-search-deepseek`'s `apiKey` — written to stderr and into crash/startup logs. The credentials provider has no JSON mode and never has this exposure.

findings.title: writeFileAtomic relies on a POSIX `mode` that Windows ignores, so .credentials.yaml inherits the user-profile DACL (which typically includes the local Users group)
findings.detail:
`writeFile(temp, content, { mode: options.mode, flag: 'wx' })` — `mode` is inert on Windows, and the caller's `dirMode: 0o700` on the preceding `mkdir` is equally inert. Every durable secret store in the product funnels through here (credentials-local L699/L720/L778/L848, settings-file L227), so on Windows both `.credentials.yaml` and `settings.yaml` are created with whatever DACL they inherit from the parent.

Under a default `%USERPROFILE%` ACL that inheritance carries the local `Users` group's read access down from `C:\Users`, meaning any local account on a shared Windows box can read every stored API key and OAuth refresh token. credentials-local's own `assertOwnerOnly()` documents this hole and skips the check on win32 rather than fixing it, so nothing compensates. The codebase already contains the correct pattern: packages/fs/fs-local/src/fsio.ts `writeFileAtomic` explicitly copies the destination's DACL onto the staging file and publishes through `replaceFileWin32` for exactly this reason (fsio.ts L567-593). The weaker helper is the one protecting the credentials.

findings.title: cloneJsonShaped assigns into an object literal, so a `__proto__` key in a settings payload is silently swallowed by the prototype setter
findings.detail:
`out` is created as `{}` and filled with `out[key] = clone(entry, ...)`. When a wire payload carries an own `__proto__` key (which `JSON.parse` produces for `{"__proto__": {...}}`), the assignment hits `Object.prototype.__proto__`'s setter: for an object value it reassigns `out`'s [[Prototype]] instead of creating an own property, and for a scalar it is discarded entirely. Either way the key never reaches the stored document, with no error.

The same `obj[key] =` shape recurs in `mergeLayers` (L302 `merged[key] = ...`) and in redact.ts (L64 `rebuilt[key] = entry`, L69 `rebuilt[key] = stripped`), so the key is dropped from the write path, the merge path and the redaction path. The contrast inside this repo is instructive: storage-sqlite/unit.ts L71 uses `Object.create(null)` precisely so record keys such as `__proto__` "land as an own property instead of mutating the prototype", and storage-json goes through Map/Object.fromEntries which are CreateDataProperty-safe. Settings is the one surface that mishandles it, and it is the one fed directly from browser RPC payloads (`settings.update` / `replace` / `mutate`). Impact is limited to that key name, so medium rather than high, but the failure is silent data loss.

findings.title: patchNode uses `key in next`, so removing a YAML settings key named toString/valueOf/constructor never reaches disk
findings.detail:
`in` walks the prototype chain. `current` comes from `document.toJS()`, so a namespace that legitimately holds a key named `toString`, `valueOf`, `constructor`, `hasOwnProperty`, etc. has it as an own property; `key in next` then returns true for `next` purely because it inherits from Object.prototype, and `document.deleteIn` is never called for it.

Result: `settings.replace(ns, {...})` or `mutate([{op:'unset', path:[...] }])` correctly updates the in-memory resolved value and bumps the revision, but the key survives on disk in settings.yaml. The next reload re-publishes the stale value, so the user's deletion silently reverts. This is narrow (only that handful of property names) but it is a real memory/disk divergence on the documented removal path.

findings.title: loadEnv applies .env with process.loadEnvFile and no bootstrap-name denylist, unlike its sibling loadLayeredEnv
findings.detail:
The product CLI path (loadLayeredEnv, L177) parses both .env layers, validates them against BOOTSTRAP_NAMES / BOOTSTRAP_PREFIXES (PATH, NODE_OPTIONS, LD_PRELOAD, BASH_ENV, GIT_SSH_COMMAND, CF_*, NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED, HTTP_PROXY, …) and throws if a file tries to set one, before applying anything. `loadEnv` does none of that — it calls `process.loadEnvFile` directly on `<cwd>/.env`, so a checked-out repository's .env can set LD_PRELOAD, NODE_OPTIONS, BASH_ENV, GIT_SSH_COMMAND or CF_* for the whole process.

`loadEnv` is currently only reached from examples/acp-demo and examples/jsonrpc-demo, which keeps it out of the shipped CLI today; but it is an exported API of the boot package, sits directly beside the guarded one, and is the obvious thing an embedder or a future bin reaches for. The asymmetry should be either a denylist or a removal.

findings.title: deleteComposition's containment guard is a raw prefix test without a path separator
findings.detail: `preset.path.startsWith(dir)` accepts any path that shares a string prefix with the writable root. With two configured `user` roots `/a/b` and `/a/b2`, a preset discovered under the second has `preset.path = /a/b2/x/agent.cordis.yml`, which passes `startsWith('/a/b')`; the function then `rm`s `join('/a/b', 'x')`, which does not exist, and `force: true` makes that a successful no-op — the caller is told the preset was deleted while the real directory stays on disk and keeps occupying the id. The failure is silent rather than destructive (rm never leaves the intended root), so this is a correctness bug in the guard, not a traversal escape; PRESET_ID already rules out `..` and separators. Compare the pattern used elsewhere in the tree, e.g. `isPathUnder` in fs-sandbox, which appends `sep` before prefixing.

find:cf-infra.summary:
Overall the cluster is well-engineered and unusually self-aware: credentials-local is meticulous about never quoting secret values into diagnostics, refuses world-readable documents on POSIX, validates the whole YAML document before accepting it, and does its read-modify-write under a cross-process lock with the reconcile correctly placed before the render; storage-json/storage-sqlite validate every identifier against UNIT_NAME_RE before interpolation, use Map / Object.create(null) so `__proto__` record keys stay data, and fs-local's atomic writer handles Windows DACLs, no-clobber publication and staging-dir cleanup properly. The weaknesses cluster in two places rather than being scattered.

The sharpest issue is in the settings write path, not the credential one: SettingsProvider.write() takes its snapshot and evaluates expectedRevision before FileSettingsProvider.persistSection() reconciles from disk, so an external edit to the same namespace — including a `role('secret')` field — is reconciled, published to watchers, and then deleted from the file by renderYaml's key-deletion pass. The credentials provider does the same shape correctly, which makes it a clear oversight rather than a design choice. The second cluster is crash/kill recovery in util/atomic-write, which every durable user-data document depends on: writeFileAtomic never fsyncs the file or the parent directory (the sibling storage-json writer does, with an explicit fsyncDirectory), and withFileLock writes the holder's pid but never reads it back, so a SIGKILL during the 30s network-round-trip credential mutation permanently wedges all credential writes until an operator deletes the lock file by hand. The third cluster is secret redaction, where redactSecrets fails open on any schema node it does not recognise and the JSON settings path hands V8's excerpt-bearing SyntaxError message to the logger and boot diagnostic — both of which quietly undercut the deliberate secrecy discipline the YAML and credential paths implement.

Remaining findings are real but narrower: a POSIX `mode` that Windows ignores leaves credentials inherited-ACL-protected, `__proto__` keys are dropped by object-literal assignment in the settings clone/merge/redact paths, `key in next` blocks deletion of prototype-named YAML keys, app-boot's legacy loadEnv bypasses the bootstrap-variable denylist its sibling enforces, and deleteComposition's containment check is a separator-less prefix test. No path traversal, symlink-following escape, or SQL/identifier injection survived verification — those surfaces are genuinely tight. There is a meaningful test gap around the lost-update scenario (settings-file's concurrency specs cover cross-namespace preservation, which is exactly the case that works, and never a same-namespace concurrent external edit), and around orphan-lock recovery.

findings.title: addToHot() hard-hangs the process once the HOT layer reaches capacity
findings.detail: addToHot() evicts in a synchronous while-loop, but evictFromHot() only removes the id from the LRU order (hotAccessOrder.shift()) — it does NOT remove it from this.hotContext. Removal from hotContext happens only inside demoteToWarm(), and that is gated behind `await this.storeInWarm(...)`, so it always resolves on a later microtask. The while-loop never yields to the microtask queue, so hotContext.size never decreases during the loop. After hotAccessOrder is drained, evictFromHot() returns false and does nothing, leaving `this.hotContext.size >= this.config.maxHotSize` permanently true. Result: an infinite synchronous spin — the event loop is starved and the process hangs with 100% CPU. Reproducible with exactly maxHotSize (default 100) distinct keys. Bonus corruption: demoteToWarm() calls getFromHot(hotId), which calls updateLRU(id) and re-pushes the just-evicted id to the tail of the LRU order before finally removing it, so even a non-hanging path would reorder LRU incorrectly.

findings.title: Default 'context-clear' stop policy can never fire — executeTask's discussion loop is unbounded
findings.detail: GodRuntime hard-codes stopPolicy: 'context-clear' (line 5646) and drives discussion with `while (shouldContinue) { ... shouldContinue = discussionResult.shouldContinue }` (line 5778) with no maxRounds, timeout, or budget guard. shouldContinueDiscussion's 'context-clear' branch is `modelCoverage < 0.9 || stability < 0.8 || roundNumber < 3` — it never consults this.maxRounds, unlike every other policy branch. `stability` is computed as `1 - (sum of claimsMade over the last 3 rounds) / (rounds * 5)`. extractClaims emits up to 3 claims per participant per round (the canned reasoning template has ≥3 sentences >20 chars), so with the minimum 2 agents claimsMade is 6/round and stability = 1 − 18/15 = −0.2, permanently below 0.8. modelCoverage saturates at 1.0 and roundNumber<3 becomes false after round 3, so the third disjunct keeps the loop alive forever. Each round appends claims/evidence and rebuilds all edges O(evidence×claims), so it is also a progressive livelock with unbounded memory growth. A MAD run under the default config never terminates.

findings.title: VerificationEngine decides pass/fail with Math.random() — the whole verification gate is a coin flip
findings.detail: Every registered check (micro-syntax, gen-security, adv-counterexample, …) has an executor that does nothing but return status:'pending'. The actual verdict comes from simulateCheckExecution(), which is `const random = Math.random(); const passed = random < basePassRate[checkDef.level]`. The artifact is never inspected (`_artifact` is unused). Consequences: (1) the same artifact flips COMPLETED/FAILED between runs — no reproducibility, no provenance; (2) the failure severity is itself random for micro/general, so even the failed/warnings split is arbitrary; (3) adversarial failures are hard-coded to severity 'warning' (never 'error'), so the adversarial tier can never fail the gate via `allFailures.some(f => f.severity === 'error')`. Full verification cascade and FinalReport.verification both inherit this.

findings.title: Gauntlet quality gate is simulated: critic verdict is Math.random(), so the gate passes by looping
findings.detail: In executeTask Phase 5 the blind critic is `winner: Math.random() > 0.3 ? 'bar' : 'artifact'` and the builder is a no-op that echoes its feedback. GauntletLoop exits as soon as `critique.winner === 'artifact' || 'tie'`, so with a 30% pass rate per round the gauntlet declares PASSED within a handful of rounds regardless of artifact quality. measureImprovement() likewise returns `Math.random() * 0.3` and discards its inputs. The advanced path (mad/utils/advanced-gauntlet.ts:496) is worse: `baseArtifactScore = 30 + (this.currentRound * 10) + (Math.random() * 20) + roundImprovement * 100` — the score is a function of the round counter, not of the artifact, so the artifact "beats the bar" purely by iterating. Neither path reads the artifact.

findings.title: Production readiness gate returns READY on three fabricated, hard-coded criteria
findings.detail: computeGateResult() builds criteriaMet with `testsPass: true`, `performanceOk: true`, `documented: true` — all literal, with the authors' own comments admitting the real checks are missing. The gate can therefore only be blocked by the ad-hoc lint heuristic; a project with failing tests and no docs still reports READY. Compounding this, runStressTestAgent() unconditionally pushes a finding titled 'Stress Test Completed' with 'No critical issues found', and checkBestPractices()/checkDocumentation() return []. This is the surface consumers rely on to decide whether to ship.

findings.title: LLMProviderManager.stream() converts a failed stream into a successful empty completion
findings.detail: stream() wraps the per-provider generator in try/catch and, on any error (HTTP 4xx/5xx, abort, network), yields a final chunk with `delta: ''` and `isFinal: true` carrying the error only in `metadata.error`, then swallows the exception. Every consumer that keys off isFinal/delta (the only fields most stream loops look at) sees a clean, successful, empty completion — no throw, no retry, no circuit-breaker trip. Combined with the `complete()` retry loop directly above (which retries all errors including non-retryable 401/400), auth failures are silently swallowed on the streaming path and blindly retried on the non-streaming path.

findings.title: StateManager rejects legal MAD pipeline configs; AdvancedMADEngine's finally block masks the original error
findings.detail: transitionTo() THROWS on any transition not in the allow-list, and executeTask awaits it at every phase. 'PLANNING' only permits ['DISCUSSING','VERIFYING','READY','ERROR'] and 'DEBUGGING' the same. So `createGODRuntime({ verification: { enabled: false }, gauntlet: { enabled: true } })` in PLAN/DEBUG mode reaches Phase 5 from PLANNING and throws `Invalid state transition: PLANNING -> GAUNTLET`; the same happens for productionSweep without verification. Separately, AdvancedMADEngine.execute() wraps everything in `catch { return {... status:'FAILED'} } finally { await this.godRuntime.shutdown() }` — shutdown() calls transitionTo('SHUTTING_DOWN') which is not reachable from IDLE, so if initialize() failed the finally throws and the promise REJECTS instead of returning the FAILED result the catch was written to provide, replacing the original cause. Finally, shutdown() sets initialized=false but leaves activeAgents populated, so the next execute() re-registers the same root ids and activeAgents grows by N every session, inflating the discussion participant list and the `agentUtilization` division at line 5922 (which is also NaN when activeAgents is empty).

findings.title: BYOK: cost is priced off the wrong map key, the budget is never enforced, and unknown-provider fallback recurses forever
findings.detail: Three defects in the credential/budget manager. (1) estimateCost does `baseRates[provider?.name.toLowerCase() ?? 'openai']` — but baseRates is keyed by provider *id* ('openai','anthropic',…) while ProviderConfig.name is the display name ('OpenAI','Google AI','Muse'). 'openai'→'openai' happens to match, but every other provider (anthropic, google, deepseek, opencode, muse, and all custom providers) falls through to the `|| 0.00003` default, so dailySpent/monthlySpent and every per-key totalCost are wrong — Anthropic is billed at the OpenAI rate. (2) Nothing anywhere calls getBudgetStatus() or blocks on it: dailySpent/monthlySpent are tracked and alerted on, but no request path refuses to run past the ceiling, so the budget is advisory only. (3) tryFallback() iterates fallbackChain and calls getKey(fallbackProvider); getKey() on a provider with zero keys calls tryFallback(fallbackProvider) again. With the default fallbackChain ['openai','anthropic','google'] and no keys registered, each entry re-enters the chain with a different failedProvider — exponential re-entry over a 3-element array (and unbounded if a custom chain contains a cycle), producing an exponential blow-up of console traffic and stack depth. Additionally, when no healthy key matches the requested model, getKey silently falls back to *unhealthy* keys carrying a different model, so a caller can be handed a key that cannot serve the requested model.

findings.title: EventBus.request leaks a permanent listener on every timeout and cross-delivers responses between concurrent callers
findings.detail: Two independent bugs in the request/response correlation. (a) The timeout branch only sets settled and rejects — it never calls unsubscribe(), so every timed-out request leaves a permanent handler registered on `${eventType}.response` forever; the handler closure (and its captured data) is never collected and keeps firing no-op checks on every subsequent response. (b) requestId is minted AFTER the subscription is installed, and the handler accepts a response whenever `!event.metadata?.requestId || event.metadata.requestId === requestId`. So a response emitted without a requestId — which is exactly what a non-cooperating responder produces — satisfies whichever pending request's handler runs first. Two concurrent request() calls for the same eventType can therefore resolve with each other's payloads, and the loser hangs until its own timeout (which then leaks per (a)).

findings.title: IntelligentCache.set() double-subtracts an entry's size when eviction selects the key being replaced
findings.detail: set() unconditionally subtracts the old entry's estimated size up front (`this.currentSize -= estimateSize(existingEntry.value)`) but leaves the stale entry in the Map. The eviction loop then runs `while (this.currentSize + size > this.maxBytes && this.cache.size > 0) evictLRU()`, and evictLRU's LRU score (`timestamp + accesses*1000`) can legitimately select that same still-present key. delete() then subtracts the old size a second time. Net effect after the write: currentSize = original − 2×old + new. Once the cache is under memory pressure this drifts monotonically negative, so the cache believes it has unbounded headroom and stops evicting — a slow unbounded-memory leak on exactly the path the maxMemoryMB cap exists to protect. maxEntries (default 10000) is declared in CacheConfig and never enforced anywhere, so entry count is also unbounded.

findings.title: PolicyAgentTreeManager.terminateAgent never removes nodes from the tree, permanently exhausting maxTotalAgents
findings.detail: terminateAgent() recursively marks descendants 'active'→'terminated' and clears childrenIds, but never deletes anything from this.agentTree. spawnChildAgent() gates on `this.agentTree.size >= this.spawnPolicy.maxTotalAgents`, and cleanupIdleAgents() (called from GodRuntime.shutdown, with the default 5-minute idle timeout) terminates agents all the time. Every terminated agent therefore continues to occupy a slot forever. After maxTotalAgents (default 20) spawn/terminate cycles — which the idle sweeper manufactures on its own — every subsequent spawnChildAgent throws 'Max total agents (20) exceeded' and the tree is permanently wedged. getActiveAgents() correctly filters by status, so getTreeStatistics() and spawn capacity disagree. A second, related bug: spawnChildAgent uses `childConfig.id || generateId()`; a duplicate configured id silently overwrites the previous node in the Map while the parent's childrenIds retains the id twice, corrupting the tree.

findings.title: Published Scheduler never tracks cost, so costUsd budgets are entirely unenforced
findings.detail: In the published @origin-ai/cf-god-runtime package, costUsed is declared (line 296), read in isExhausted() (line 326) and snapshot() (line 333), and never written by anything. reserveResources(agentCount, tokens) checks and increments only concurrency and tokens — it never consults budgets.costUsd. So a BudgetPolicy of { costUsd: 0.01 } is accepted (the constructor's 'at least one ceiling' check passes) and then never trips. Since GodRuntime.checkProgress() is defined as `!this.scheduler.isExhausted()`, the progress gate that is supposed to stop a run when budget is exhausted can never fire on cost. releaseResources(_agentId) also ignores its argument and blindly decrements, so an unmatched release silently inflates free capacity. Adjacent in the same package: Router.eligibilityReason() explicitly ignores requiredTools/permissions/capability/contextWindow (line 206-218 — only available/healthy are checked) and DiscussionBus.mustContinue() is hardcoded `return true` (discussion-bus/src/index.ts:216) with no timeout or budget guard, so the bus's documented 'timeout + budget guard' does not exist.

find:cf-orchestration.summary:
Scope note: the declared review paths (packages/core, packages/mad, packages/workflow, packages/subagent) contain mostly thin published stubs; the real MAD orchestration heart named in the hotspot list lives in packages/cf/src/{mad,iwin,byok}.ts. I reviewed both, prioritizing the hotspots. Overall health of this cluster is poor at the orchestration layer and good at the session/subagent layer.

The MAD core (god-runtime.ts, 6475 lines, 26 inlined classes) is a simulation wearing the clothes of a production system. The three gates that consumers are meant to trust — verification, gauntlet, and production-readiness — are respectively a coin flip, a round-counter, and three hard-coded `true` literals; the docs, class names and FinalReport fields all claim otherwise. On top of that, the default discussion stop policy mathematically cannot terminate, and the HOT memory layer hard-hangs the process at capacity. Together these mean a default MAD run either never finishes or finishes with fabricated quality signal.

Concurrency-wise the picture is mixed. The EventBus request/response correlation leaks a listener per timeout and cross-delivers between concurrent callers; the byok fallback chain recurses; the GodRuntime state machine throws on configurations that the config surface openly advertises; and the published Scheduler never enforces its cost budget at all. Cancellation is largely decorative — GauntletLoop.stop() is a no-op because shouldContinueGauntlet never reads isRunning, and I-WIN's pause()/enabled flag are likewise ignored by shouldContinue().

By contrast, packages/core/session, packages/core/agent, packages/subagent/subagent (continuation.ts) are carefully written: explicit cycle guards (liveLineage's `seen` set), documented send-versus-dispose cutoffs, and non-reentrant drain logic. I found nothing reportable there.

Also worth flagging but below the cut: packages/cf/src/mad/utils/examples.ts has a missing paren at line 243 producing 67 syntax errors — the package's own `npm run typecheck` exits 2, so the typecheck CI gate is already red. mad/utils/advanced-verification.ts uses stateful /g regexes with `.test()` in loops (debugRegex:515, anyPattern:977) and misses roughly every other matching line — todoRegex at 497 is accidentally saved by the `.match()` on the following line resetting lastIndex. Scheduler.topologicalSort() has no cycle detection, so a cyclic task graph is silently accepted and the tasks stall in 'pending' forever. MemoryFabricManager.addToHot (god-runtime:4055) calls the async demoteToWarm() without await from a sync method, so warm writes are unordered and rejections are unhandled. AdvancedMADEngine.execute discards the caught error entirely — the returned FAILED result carries no error message, so callers cannot distinguish a bad task from a crashed runtime.

findings.title: `--host 0.0.0.0` is rejected only as a CLI string literal; the webserver still accepts an all-interfaces bind and then auto-trusts every LAN IPv4
findings.detail: The safety rail is a single string comparison inside the commander action of `cf --profile web`. The `WebServer` service still declares `0.0.0.0` as a legal config value (`packages/host/webserver/src/index.ts:61,75`), so any other composition path — a `cordis.yml`/`cordis.patch.yml` overlay, an embedder constructing the service directly, or a future caller that sets `host` from somewhere other than this one flag — binds all interfaces with no refusal. When the bind host *is* `0.0.0.0`, `resolveLanTrust` then enumerates every non-internal IPv4 on the machine and appends them all to the `/api` browser-trust fence's `trustedHosts`. Those are port-less entries, so they match the Host on **any** port. Net effect of reaching an all-interfaces bind by any route other than the CLI literal: the full RPC surface (`session.prompt`, `host.openPath`, `credentials.set`, …) is reachable from every device on the LAN with no authentication — the exact outcome the error message says it prevents. The check belongs in the webserver's schema (or `resolveLanTrust`), not in one argv parse.

findings.title: No security headers on any static response, and no CSP in the web app document
findings.detail: `content-type` is the only header ever set on the SPA surface. There is no `Content-Security-Policy`, no `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, no `Referrer-Policy`, and no `frame-ancestors`/`X-Frame-Options` anywhere in the serving path (grep over the whole repo for these names returns nothing), and `apps/web/index.html` carries no CSP `<meta>`. The document renders LLM-authored markdown and sits in the same origin as an RPC surface that can run shell commands as the host user, so there is zero output-side containment if a renderer bug ever slips through — the markdown renderer itself looks sound (protocol allowlist, raw HTML kept as literal text, shiki escaping), making this defense-in-depth rather than an open hole. The fix is real but not free: `renderIndexInjections` splices inline `<script>` rows into the head and body, so a CSP must allow `'unsafe-inline'` for scripts until those rows are nonced or externalized; `script-src 'self'` alone would work for everything else since the loader uses `import()`, not `eval`. `nosniff` is free and should ship regardless.
