find:cf-cli.summary: apps/cli is a thin, well-documented launcher (6 source files, ~995 lines) whose arg grammar in args.ts is careful and largely correct — pass-through boundary, dump validations, and the mutual-exclusion checks all behave as documented, verified by driving the real `parseCfArgs`. The problems concentrate in `cf plugin`, the weakest-tested surface: its win32 `shell: true` npm forwarder concatenates unescaped user argv into a cmd.exe command line (space-splitting breaks the documented `anchorPathSpec` anchoring, `%VAR%` expands, and `>` silently writes a file into the profile directory — all reproduced), and the same shell choice makes the `ENOENT` "npm not found" branch provably unreachable on the only platform that sets `shell`, yielding a wrong message and a wrong exit code. `cf plugin` also never runs the one-way legacy `~/.dsh` migration while being the command that first creates `~/.cf`, permanently stranding legacy data; and it has no help surface at all because the root's `.helpOption(false)` is inherited. The next tier is error/UX correctness: bin.ts has no error boundary and profile-boot's `installFailLoud` listens only for `unhandledRejection`, which a rejected top-level await never emits, so ordinary config failures print raw V8 stacks; `rejectParentOptions('plugin')` is shadowed by commander's mandatory-option check and never fires; the launcher's own `agent-presets` overlay clobbers `roots` rather than appending to it; and an out-of-range `result.status` is passed straight to `process.exit`. No security-critical or data-corrupting defects beyond the legacy-migration skip; exit codes are correct in every case tested. The test suite covers the web/headless/dump/boot paths well but has no coverage for plugin help, npm-missing, or space-bearing path specs — precisely the three paths that are broken.

findings.title: Safetensors loader: heap OOB read from untrusted shape/data_offsets (no numel*bpe vs raw.size() check)
findings.detail: load_safetensors trusts two fully attacker-controlled fields independently and never cross-checks them. `shape` drives `numel` (line 226-227) and thus `at.data.resize(numel)`, while `data_offsets` drives the size of the staging buffer `raw` (line 244). There is no check that `off_end - off_start >= numel * bpe`, no check that `data_start + off_start`/`off_end` lies inside `file_size`, and no check of `f.gcount()` after the read. A crafted header such as `{"w":{"dtype":"F32","shape":[10000000],"data_offsets":[0,4]}}` yields numel=10,000,000 and raw.size()=4; the loop then takes `&raw[i*4]` for i up to 1e7 and reads ~40 MB past a 4-byte heap allocation. That is a guaranteed heap over-read (crash on guard pages, otherwise leaking adjacent heap into the converted weights). The same gap lets `off_end` be set to ~2^62, making `std::vector<uint8_t> raw((size_t)(off_end - off_start))` attempt an exabyte allocation and throw std::bad_alloc out of an API that documents no-throw. Negative `off_start` also passes the `off_end <= off_start` guard and wraps to a huge `size_t` byte_off. Note gguf_bridge.cpp does this correctly (line 361 checks `nbytes > file_size - abs_off`); the safetensors path has no equivalent.

findings.title: ModelServer::worker_loop: null model_ produces an undersized logits tensor that is then indexed as [B, max_seq_len, V], then dereferenced
findings.detail: When `model_` is null — ModelServer can be constructed with a null Model*, and `unload_model()` (line 690) sets `model_ = nullptr` while workers are still running — the fallback allocates `Tensor(Shape{B, 1, 32000})`, i.e. B*32000 floats. But the consumer at line 748-749 computes `logits.data<float>() + consolidated.offsets[i] * V + last_pos * V`, where `offsets[i] == i * max_seq_len` and max_seq_len is the longest prompt in the batch. With any prompt longer than one token, or any batch of size > 1, that index lands far past the end of the B*V allocation: an out-of-bounds read of arbitrary heap, producing garbage tokens rather than an error. Immediately after, line 761 calls `model_->forward(...)` unconditionally inside the decode loop, which is a null-pointer dereference the first time the per-request decode loop iterates. The root cause is that `model_` is a bare `Model*` written by unload_model() with no synchronization while worker_loop reads it, so even the `if (model_)` guard at line 719 is a data race. The logits shape contract is confirmed in src/model/model.cpp:104-106 (`h.reshape(Shape{B, S, config.hidden_size})` then `lm_head->forward`), so real forwards are [B,S,V] and the fallback must be too.

findings.title: ModelServer::worker_loop: empty prompt_ids underflows last_pos to -1 and reads before the logits buffer
findings.detail: `last_pos` is computed as `(int64_t)req.prompt_ids.size() - 1`. `ModelServer::submit(const ServingRequest&)` (line 620-627) enqueues the caller's struct verbatim and never enforces a non-empty prompt_ids; only the string overload at line 645 has the `if (req.prompt_ids.empty()) req.prompt_ids.push_back(1);` guard. A caller using the ServingRequest overload (the primary batching API, and the one whose `max_tokens`/`priority`/`id` members are also left uninitialized by the struct's default constructor) can therefore submit a request with an empty prompt_ids, giving last_pos = -1. `row` then points V floats *before* the start of the logits allocation, and `sampler.greedy(row, V)` reads that out-of-bounds region. consolidate_batch (line 605-613) will happily build a [B, max_seq_len] input with max_seq_len=0 for that batch, so this is reachable without any other guard firing.

findings.title: TelemetryWriter owns a raw Impl* with an implicitly-generated copy constructor: copy = double free; append() after close() = null deref
findings.detail: TelemetryWriter holds `Impl* impl_` (raw owning pointer, `new Impl` in the constructor at line 176, `delete impl_` in close()/destructor at line 213-219) and declares no copy/move constructor, no copy/move assignment, and no deleted copies. The implicit copy constructor therefore shallow-copies `impl_`, so any copy (passing the writer by value, storing it in a container, returning it from a factory) makes two objects that both `delete` the same Impl in their destructors — a double free, and a use-after-free for whichever object survives. `close()` also sets `impl_ = nullptr` without guarding subsequent calls: `append()` at line 196 does `impl_->file << ...` and `impl_->last_hash` unconditionally, so a write after close() is a null-pointer dereference. The class is a natural candidate to hold in a container or pass around, and it is exported from the header with no rule-of-five declared, so the compiler is silently generating the unsafe operations. Same shape of bug that quant_refcheck-style audits elsewhere in this tree flag as silent heap corruption.

findings.title: st_f16_to_f32 is wrong by a factor of 8192 for every normal FP16 value — every F16 safetensors checkpoint silently corrupts
findings.detail: The local `st_f16_to_f32` used at line 252 for all F16 tensors computes the normal case as `((mant|0x400) / 8388608.0f) * ldexp(1.0f, exp - 15)`. The significand must be `(mant|0x400) / 1024.0f` (i.e. 1.mant); dividing by 8388608 = 2^23 instead of 1024 = 2^10 makes every normal value 8192x too small. Concrete: fp16 0x3C00 (1.0) decodes to 1/8192 ≈ 1.22e-4, and 0x4000 (2.0) decodes to 2^-12 ≈ 2.44e-4, instead of 1.0 and 2.0. The subnormal branch is wrong in the opposite direction: it returns `mant / 16384.0f * 2.0f` = mant * 2^-13, whereas a fp16 subnormal is mant * 2^-24, so subnormals come out 2048x too large. The correct implementation already exists in the same directory as `adapters::fp16_to_float` (adapter_core.cpp:25-39, `f = (float)(mant | 0x400) / 1024.0f; ldexp(f, exp - 15)`), is declared in adapter_core.h, is used correctly by ptq_bridge.cpp:48, and is unit-tested in test_adapter_bridges.cpp:37-43 — but safetensors_bridge.cpp carries a private broken duplicate that no test covers. Result: any FP16 safetensors checkpoint (the overwhelmingly common HF format) converts to garbage weights with no error, producing a wrong-but-plausible model.

findings.title: FP8 E4M3 decoder maps exp==15 to INFINITY, but codes 0x78-0x7E are finite normals up to 448
findings.detail: OCP FP8 E4M3 has no infinity encoding: exponent field 15 with mantissa 0..6 encodes the finite values 256, 288, 320, 352, 384, 416, 448, and only 0x7F (mantissa 7) is NaN. `fp8_e4m3_to_float` returns `mant ? NAN : INFINITY` for the entire exp==15 bucket, so codes 0x78..0x7E decode to +/-INF instead of their finite values, and 0x78 (the maximum representable magnitude) decodes to INF rather than 448. These are precisely the outlier weights that block-wise FP8 scaling exists to preserve. Once one INF enters a tensor it propagates: the block max-abs scale in load_block_fp8_pair / the downstream max-abs dequant path becomes INF, and every weight in that block collapses to NaN, silently destroying the converted model. safetensors_bridge.cpp:101-106 documents that this function is the "verified" decoder it now delegates to (the L059 fix), so both files share the defect. Same structure as the L059 bug it claims to have fixed.

findings.title: detect_format allocates up to 1 GiB from the first 8 bytes of a file to decide the format
findings.detail: `detect_format` reads the first 8 bytes, interprets them as a little-endian header length, and — on the strength of `hdr_len < (1ULL << 30)` alone — heap-allocates a `std::vector<char>` of that size before reading anything: `std::vector<char> hdr((size_t)hdr_len);`. Any file whose first 8 bytes are e.g. `00 00 00 00 FF FF FF 01` forces a ~33 MB allocation, and `00 00 00 00 FF FF FF 3F` forces a full 1 GiB allocation, from a file that can be 9 bytes long. The subsequent `gcount() == hdr_len` check means this is not a correctness bug, but it is an unbounded-allocation DoS on an untrusted-input path: detect_format is the entry point that every adapter import (quant_import, gguf/safetensors dispatch) and every ModelZoo scan calls, so repeated invocation with crafted files drives the process to the OOM killer. The 1 GiB ceiling is not a defense; a sane safetensors header cap is on the order of 100 MB, and the sibling load_block_fp8_pair (safetensors_bridge.cpp:312) already uses a much tighter `1u << 26`.

findings.title: release_slot() decrements the admission counter even when the matching try_acquire_slot() never incremented it
findings.detail: try_acquire_slot() and release_slot() each re-read `max_concurrent_` independently at call time instead of recording whether a slot was actually taken. try_acquire_slot returns true early with no increment when `cap <= 0` (line 284), and release_slot returns early with no decrement under the same condition (line 303) — but they read the cap at different moments. If an operator lowers max_concurrent_ to 0 while requests are in flight, `set_max_concurrent(0)` resets the counter to 0; if the cap is then raised back to N before those in-flight requests finish, their `release_slot` calls see cap > 0 and execute `current_requests_.fetch_sub(1)` for slots that were never counted, driving `current_requests_` negative. Once negative, the CAS loop in try_acquire_slot (`while (cur < cap)`) admits extra requests, and the deficit persists — the concurrency cap silently stops working, which is exactly the protection the DoS path depends on. The symmetric toggle (N -> 0 -> N) repeats the drift. Neither direction is recoverable, because set_max_concurrent only zeroes the counter when the new limit is itself 0. `handle_request` should acquire a bool and release through a small RAII guard keyed on that bool, not on a re-read of live config.

findings.title: 431 (header-too-large) and 414 (request-line-too-long) are enforced only after the receive loop, so they do not bound memory at all
findings.detail: The read loop at line 725-809 keeps calling recv and appending to `buf` until the headers are complete or `buf.size() >= max_body` (4 MiB default). The `max_header_bytes_` (431) and `kMaxRequestLineBytes` (414) checks sit at line 827-845, i.e. *after* the loop has already buffered everything and after the full body has been read. Consequently an attacker who sends 4 MiB of header bytes with no CRLFCRLF gets to force each of the N worker threads to hold 4 MiB (4*N MiB total) before the 431 is even considered, and the 431 limit has no effect on peak memory whatsoever. The header cap is advertised in http_server.h as the control that bounds request-header memory (`Header cap: total header bytes beyond max_header_bytes_ get 431`), but as implemented it is purely a post-hoc status code. The check needs to move inside the loop — reject as soon as the accumulated bytes before the first CRLFCRLF exceed max_header_bytes_, or as soon as the request line exceeds kMaxRequestLineBytes — so the limit actually caps the allocation.

findings.title: ContinualTrainer reads batch_size*seq_len floats from a sample that train() only requires to have >= 2 elements
findings.detail: `train()` (line 21-26) only rejects a sample when `train_data[idx].size() < 2`, then hands `train_data[idx].data()` to `train_step_continual` as `input`/`target`. That function computes `flat = batch_size * seq_len` — 8 * 512 = 4096 with the default ContinualConfig — and uses `input` for `flat` elements: `new_loss += input[i]*input[i]` (line 65-67), `sample.input.assign(input, input + flat)` (line 108), `sample.target.assign(target, target + flat)` (line 109), and `old_logits_.assign(input, input + flat)` (line 115). `target` is `train_data[idx].data() + half`, so the copy at line 109 walks `flat` elements starting halfway through the sample. With any sample smaller than ~1.5*flat this is a heap over-read of the sample vector, and the over-read data is then stored into the replay buffer and reused for distillation. The only precondition the public `train()` API documents is a non-empty vector; with defaults, samples under ~6 KB trip it. Two further crashers in the same file: `s % train_data.size()` at line 22 and line 30 divides by zero when `train_data` is empty (the function has no emptiness guard), and `new_loss /= (double)flat` at line 68 plus `replay_l /= (double)rbatch` at line 81 divide by zero when batch_size or seq_length is 0.

findings.title: PluginManager::hot_reload calls load_from_dll() outside plugins_mutex_, but load_from_dll pushes to entries_ unlocked
findings.detail: The bug-census comment on hot_reload correctly fixes the old self-deadlock (holding plugins_mutex_ then calling load(), which re-locks the same non-recursive mutex), but the replacement goes too far the other way: it releases the lock at line 155 and then calls `load_from_dll(path)` at line 156 with no lock held. `load_from_dll` is not lock-free — its success path does `entries_.push_back(entry)` (line 49 on Windows, line 72 on POSIX) with no synchronization of its own. Only `load()` is documented to take the lock around that call. So a concurrent `hot_reload` and `load`/`unload`/`unload_all`, or two concurrent `hot_reload`s, mutate the same `std::vector<PluginEntry>` concurrently: a real data race on the vector's backing store, with push_back reallocation invalidating iterators that `unload` and `on_generate_start`/`on_token_generated`/`on_generate_end` are walking under their own (different, non-overlapping) lock scopes. Those three snapshot loops copy raw `Plugin*` out of `entries_` and then invoke plugin callbacks after releasing the lock, so a `hot_reload` racing them can FreeLibrary a handle whose Plugin is mid-callback. Fix: either take the lock inside load_from_dll (and keep hot_reload's outer scope closed around it), or split it into an unlocked `load_from_dll_locked` variant plus a documented contract.

findings.title: write_quant_mixed materializes every quantized block in RAM before writing, enabling a 400 GB transient allocation from a single 4 GB tensor
findings.detail: `write_quant_mixed` is the mandatory conversion funnel for every external format ("NOTHING leaves the adapter edition in a foreign format"), and it buffers the *entire* converted model in memory before writing a single byte: `all_blocks` holds a BlockData per block with its own `std::vector<uint8_t> indices` and `std::vector<uint8_t> codebook` (line 339), populated for every block of every tensor (line 371-375) before `write_format_table`/`write_tensor_table`/`write_block` run at line 402-404. A 1B-parameter FP32 checkpoint is 4 GB of input, and at ~2.6 BPW the staging vectors hold ~325 MB of payload plus a per-block heap allocation (~4M separate allocations at block_size=256) plus the FormatBlockEntry/TensorEntry tables — so peak RSS is input + staging, not input. At 10B parameters this exceeds RAM on a typical workstation and terminates via std::bad_alloc with a partially-written .quant file left on disk (the header and tables are never written, but the file is created and truncated by the QUANTWriter constructor). The on-disk format is strictly sequential — header, then format table, then tensor table, then blocks — so this can be streamed: quantize a block and write it immediately, or at minimum two-pass (count, then write) with a bounded block window. The `all_blocks.reserve(tensors.size() * 4)` at line 340 is also unbounded in the same way: a safetensors file declaring a 100 GB tensor makes `at.data.resize(numel)` throw before reserve is reached, but a file declaring 100M tiny tensors makes `reserve(400M)` attempt ~9.6 GB for the capacity alone.

find:tf-server.summary: Reviewed the server layer (http_server.cpp, json_parser.cpp, production_api/core/gen), the adapter bridge tree (gguf/safetensors/ptq/delta/continual/mtp + adapter_core), and the GLE telemetry module against the request-parsing / validation / allocation / threading checklist. The tree is clearly mid-hardening and many previous bug-census findings genuinely are fixed (chunked TE fails closed, stoll is caught, JSON recursion is capped in json_parser.cpp, GGUF tensor byte ranges are validated, hot_reload's self-deadlock is gone), so the baseline is better than the file counts suggest. But the fixes are unevenly applied, and three themes account for essentially all of the serious findings. First, untrusted-input validation is present in one bridge and missing in its twin: gguf_bridge.cpp checks every tensor's byte range against file_size before reading, while safetensors_bridge.cpp trusts shape and data_offsets independently and indexes a heap buffer by numel*bpe with no bound check at all — a straight heap over-read from a crafted file, and the single most urgent fix here. Second, there are three independent copies of the same numeric decoders and only some are correct: the codebase already contains a correct fp16_to_float that is tested, but safetensors_bridge ships a private duplicate that is wrong by 8192x for every normal value, so every F16 checkpoint silently converts to garbage with no error — exactly the wrong-but-plausible-model class the brief targets. Third, shared mutable state is guarded inconsistently: ModelServer's model_ is a bare pointer that unload_model() nulls under no lock while workers dereference it, PluginManager::hot_reload correctly escapes its own lock and then calls a function that mutates the guarded vector unlocked, and the HTTP admission counter can be driven negative by a set_max_concurrent toggle, disabling the concurrency cap. Beyond those, detect_format allocates up to 1 GiB from eight attacker-controlled bytes on every import dispatch, the 431/414 header limits are checked only after the receive loop and therefore bound nothing, ContinualTrainer reads 4096 floats from samples its own API only requires to have two, TelemetryWriter's raw owning pointer has an implicitly-generated copy constructor, and write_quant_mixed holds an entire converted model in RAM before writing a byte. GGUF's dequantizers turned out to be faithful and in-bounds on close inspection (q2_k and q6_k read exactly to the last byte of their block vectors), so the block-codec path is in better shape than its raw-pointer density suggests.

findings.title: avx2_gemm / avx2_tiled_gemm contract B incorrectly and compute the wrong matrix product
findings.detail:
Both AVX2 kernels load B with `_mm256_loadu_ps(B + k*N + n)`, which reads 8 *contiguous* floats along B's row (the N direction), then pairs lane j with `a_row[k+j]` (the K direction). Lane j therefore accumulates A[m][k+j]*B[k][n+j], and the horizontal sum over the 8 lanes folds N into the result: sum = Σ_k Σ_j A[m][k+j]*B[k][n+j]. The correct result is Σ_k A[m][k]*B[k][n] (see `scalar_gemm` at line 19 in the same file, which is the reference). The two agree only when N==1 or K<8 (the scalar tail). A strided gather with stride N is required, not a contiguous load.

Concrete counterexample: M=1,N=2,K=8 gives computed C[0][0]=A0B0+A1B1+...+A7B7 instead of A0B0+A1B2+A2B4+...+A7B14.

Reachable: `src/backend/backend.cpp:155` calls `kernel::avx2_gemm(...)` from `CPUAVX2Backend::gemm`, the advertised CPU AVX2 backend. `avx2_tiled_gemm` (line 144, identical load) has the same defect. No live caller was found for `avx2_tiled_gemm`.

findings.title: VkPhysicalDeviceMemoryProperties declares memoryTypes fields in the wrong order, so every memory-type query reads heapIndex as propertyFlags
findings.detail:
Real Vulkan `VkMemoryType` is `{ VkMemoryPropertyFlags propertyFlags; uint32_t heapIndex; }` — propertyFlags at offset 0, heapIndex at offset 4. This hand-rolled ABI mirror declares the pair as `{ uint32_t heapIndex; VkFlags propertyFlags; }` (offsets 0 and 4), so reading `.propertyFlags` actually returns the driver's **heapIndex**, and `.heapIndex` returns **propertyFlags**. Total struct size and the memoryHeapCount offset still line up, so the bug is invisible to a size check.

Consequences (both live):
- `igpu_zero_copy.cpp:845-855 has_unified_memory()` tests `(props & HOST_VISIBLE) && (props & HOST_COHERENT) && (props & DEVICE_LOCAL)` against heapIndex, which is 0 or 1, so the conjunction is essentially never true. `IGPUZeroCopyAllocator::init()` then sets `cpu_fallback = true` and the integrated-GPU zero-copy path silently disables itself on hardware that supports it.
- `igpu_zero_copy.cpp:703-709` and `gpu_compute_vulkan.cpp:915-920 find_memory_type()` filter on the wrong field, so `allocate_unified()` (line 929-950) can bind a memory type that is **not** HOST_VISIBLE and then call `vkMapMemory` on it — a VUID violation that is undefined behavior in the driver, not a clean error.

findings.title: VkPipelineShaderStageCreateInfo.sType hardcoded to 5 instead of 18 on the iGPU zero-copy path
findings.detail:
`VK_STRUCTURE_TYPE_PIPELINE_SHADER_STAGE_CREATE_INFO` is 18. The value 5 is `VK_STRUCTURE_TYPE_DEVICE_CREATE_INFO`. The iGPU zero-copy backend still passes 5 into `vkCreateComputePipelines`, so the driver reads the create-info through the wrong struct interpretation and the call fails validation (or misbehaves) for every pipeline in `pipeline_cache`.

This is not a new guess — the identical bug was already found and fixed in the sibling backend, and the fix comment is still in the tree there. `gpu_compute_vulkan.cpp:894` now reads `ssi.sType = VK_STRUCTURE_TYPE_PIPELINE_SHADER_STAGE_CREATE_INFO;   // 18, was 0x5`. `igpu_zero_copy.cpp` was never given the same fix.

`get_pipeline()` is called on the dispatch path for every compute shader in the zero-copy backend.

findings.title: param_map_ is guarded by two different mutexes — unregister_parameter uses param_mutex_, everything else uses mutex_
findings.detail:
`param_map_` is a single `std::unordered_map` protected inconsistently:
- `unregister_parameter()` (line 24) locks `param_mutex_`. This is the function invoked from `Tensor::~Tensor` via `detail::autograd_unregister_hook`, so it runs whenever any registered-parameter Tensor dies, including on worker threads.
- `register_parameter()` (line 327), `backward()` (line 367, which does `param_map_.find()` at 414/420/426), and `clear()` (line 460) all lock `mutex_` instead.
- Only `reset()` (lines 471-472) locks both.

Because the two paths take different locks, a Tensor being destroyed on thread B mutates `param_map_` concurrently with `backward()` or `register_parameter()` on thread A: concurrent `unordered_map` insert/erase/find is a data race and can invalidate iterators mid-lookup or free a node still being read. `clear()` also leaves `param_map_` populated with live `Tensor*` entries (deliberately, per the comment at 464-466) that `backward()` dereferences at line 426 after only an address-equality check, so a stale entry that aliases a reallocated Tensor still passes.

findings.title: Tensor::copy_from / copy_to validate only numel, never dtype, so memcpy length is taken from the destination and can overflow the source
findings.detail:
`copy_from` checks that the two tensors have the same element count and then does `memcpy(data(), src.data(), size_bytes())`, where `size_bytes()` is `numel() * dtype_size(dtype_)` of `*this*` (tensor.h:51). Nothing compares `dtype_` with `src.dtype_`.

- If src is F16 (2 B/elem) and dst is F32 (4 B/elem) with equal numel, the copy reads twice src's allocation → heap over-read.
- If src is F32 and dst is F16, it writes twice dst's allocation → heap overflow.
- If the dtype is an unrecognized value, `dtype_size` returns 0 (`types.h:290`), so `size_bytes()` is 0 and the copy silently does nothing while reporting success.

This is a public API used by `Tensor::copy_to`, and by `void copy(...)` in roughly a dozen ComputeBackend implementations in `src/backend/backend.cpp` (lines 128, 218, 265, 533, 695, 856, 1020, 1102, 1178, ...), where src and dst come from caller-controlled tensors.

findings.title: Safetensors loader never checks data_offsets size against the tensor's declared shape, so a malformed checkpoint drives an out-of-bounds heap read
findings.detail:
The loader derives `numel` from the JSON `shape` (line 226-228) and `raw` from the JSON `data_offsets` (line 244) but never cross-checks them. There is also no check that `data_start + off_end <= file_size`, and no check that `f.read` actually filled the buffer.

So a checkpoint declaring `shape=[1024,1024]` with `dtype=F32` but `data_offsets=[8,100]` allocates a 92-byte `raw` vector and then runs the decode loop for 1048576 elements, doing `const uint8_t* p = &raw[(size_t)i * bpe]; memcpy(&v, p, 4);` — a multi-megabyte out-of-bounds heap read of attacker-controlled length. A truncated file has the same effect because `raw` keeps its requested size and is left partly uninitialized.

`off_start` also comes from `atoll` and can be negative, which is then added into `size_t byte_off = (size_t)(data_start + off_start)` before `seekg`.

Contrast `gguf_bridge.cpp:347-353`, which does validate: `if (abs_off > (uint64_t)file_size || nbytes > (uint64_t)file_size - abs_off)`. Safetensors has no equivalent. This is the primary untrusted-input path into model loading.

findings.title: slice() and transpose() accept negative dims and start>end, producing out-of-bounds Shape writes and a negative numel that wraps size_bytes()
findings.detail:
`Tensor::slice(int dim, ...)` checks only `dim < shape_.rank` — a negative `dim` passes. It then evaluates `shape_.dims[dim]` and assigns `t.shape_.dims[dim] = end - start`, both of which index out of the fixed `int64_t dims[8]` array (Shape is declared `int64_t dims[8]; int rank;` in types.h:306, so `dims[-1]` reads/writes the memory immediately preceding the Shape object). `Tensor::transpose(dim1, dim2)` at line 182 has the same `dim < rank`-only check and then does `std::swap(t.shape_.dims[dim1], t.shape_.dims[dim2])`.

Separately, `slice` never asserts `start <= end`. When `start > end` the extent is negative, `Shape::numel()` multiplies out negative, and `size_bytes()` (tensor.h:51) computes `numel() * dtype_size(...)` where a negative int64_t converts to a huge size_t — any subsequent memcpy/loop runs off into the heap.

Both are reachable from the tensor-parallel managers, which compute `start = rank * chunk` with no clamp against the dimension: `tensor_parallelism.cpp:30-35`, `:48-50`, `:163-168`, `:521-525` and `distributed.cpp:176-190`. With more ranks than elements, `start` exceeds the dim and `end = std::min(start+chunk, total)` comes back smaller than `start`. Note that `Shape` already ships a bounds-checked `operator[]` that rejects negative indices — `slice`/`transpose` bypass it by indexing the raw array.

findings.title: copy_from / clone / fill / zero_ / serialize ignore contiguity; is_contiguous() is defined but never consulted
findings.detail:
Every mutating and copying op on `Tensor` indexes `data()[i]` flat: `copy_from` (tensor.cpp:261), `clone` (271), `fill` (219-249), `zero_` (256), `serialize` (331), `to_dtype` (42-51), and every kernel in the tree. `Tensor::is_contiguous()` exists at tensor.cpp:356 and correctly detects both `offset_ != 0` and non-row-major strides, but a repo-wide grep shows nothing ever calls it.

The consequence is that any non-contiguous view is silently misinterpreted as a flat buffer. The concrete case in-tree: `TensorParallelManager::row_parallel_split` (line 48-50) and `TensorParallelWrapper::row_split` (distributed.cpp:185-190) do `weight.slice(1, start, end)` on a `{out_dim, in_dim}` weight. That yields shape `{out_dim, end-start}` with `offset_ = start*4` and strides `{in_dim, 1}` — i.e. genuinely strided. Every downstream matmul then reads `local_weight.data<float>()` over `local_weight.numel()` flat elements, which is a contiguous run starting at row 0 column `start` and spilling across row boundaries. The sharded weight is wrong while still looking well-formed.

(The same class of hazard applies to any `reshape`/`view` of a slice: `view()` at tensor.cpp:149 only compares `numel`, never contiguity, unlike `TensorView::reshape` in tensor_view.h:50 which asserts it.)

findings.title: CPUAVX2Backend::gemm derives M/N/K from A and B independently and never validates that C and B are large enough
findings.detail:
`gemm` computes `M = A.numel()/A.dim(last)`, `K = A.dim(last)`, `N = B.dim(last)` with no check that `B.numel() == K*N` and no check that `C.numel() >= M*N`. It then hands the raw pointers to `kernel::avx2_gemm`, which writes exactly `M*N` floats to C and reads `K*N` floats from B. A caller that passes a C smaller than M*N — or a B that is not `{K,N}` — gets a heap overflow with no diagnostic. `CPUAVX512Backend::gemm` has the same shape-inference pattern.

`C_orig.copy_from(C)` at line 154 is the only use of C's own shape, and it is itself unchecked against the M*N that follows.

findings.title: gemv_quant4_tiled_avx2 reads x[k+16..k+19] past the end of the activation vector, and double-counts k+4..k+15
findings.detail:
The AVX2 quant4 GEMV steps `k` by 16 under the guard `k + 16 <= K`, but loads `a3 = _mm256_loadu_ps(x + k + 12)`, i.e. x[k+12..k+19]. On the final iteration `k + 16 == K`, so x[k+16..k+19] is 4 floats (16 bytes) past the end of the activation buffer. This fires on every K that is a multiple of 16 — the common padded shape.

Separately, the four gather windows overlap: idx0 covers k+0..k+7, idx1 k+4..k+11, idx2 k+8..k+15, idx3 k+12..k+15 plus 4 lanes of `_mm_srli_si128` shift-out zeros. Paired with a0..a3 = x[k..k+7], x[k+4..k+11], x[k+8..k+15], x[k+12..k+19], weights for k+4..k+15 are each applied twice and the last 4 lanes multiply `centroids[0]` by the out-of-range activations. The scalar reference `gemv_quant4_tiled_scalar` (line 84) has neither problem.

No in-tree caller of `gemv_quant4_tiled` was found — it is compiled into `quant_kernel` and exported from `include/quant/kernel_production.h`, so this is a live defect in shipped kernel code that is currently only reachable by downstream users.

findings.title: gemv_quant8_tiled_avx2 pairs 7 of its 8 gather groups with the wrong activation slice
findings.detail:
The kernel loads 32 indices at once and builds 8 gather groups, then pairs them `w0*a0, w1*a1, w2*a2, w3*a3, w4*a0, w5*a1, w6*a2, w7*a3` with a0..a3 = x[k..k+7], x[k+8..k+15], x[k+16..k+23], x[k+24..k+31]. But the groups are not the disjoint 8-wide blocks that pairing assumes:

- idx0 = bytes 0..7  → k+0..k+7   (correct against a0)
- idx1 = bytes 4..11 → k+4..k+11  (paired with a1 = x[k+8..k+15]) — wrong
- idx2 = bytes 8..15 → k+8..k+15  (paired with a2) — wrong
- idx3 = bytes 12..15 + 4 zero bytes from `_mm_srli_si128(idx128,12)` — wrong, and 4 lanes gather codebook[0]
- idx4..idx6 similarly shifted, idx7 = bytes 28..31 + 4 zeros — wrong

Only `idx0*a0` is correct. The correct pairing needs only idx0/idx2/idx4/idx6 against a0..a3; idx1, idx3, idx5, idx7 are overlapping windows that should not be used at all. The scalar reference `gemv_quant8_tiled_scalar` (line 104) does `sum += codebook[w_row[k]] * x[k]` and is correct, so the AVX2 path diverges from the reference whenever `detect_cpu_isa() >= 2`.

Like the quant4 kernel, no in-tree caller was found; it is exported and compiled into `quant_kernel`.

findings.title: transpose()'s no-clone fast path returns a non-contiguous view that every consumer then indexes flat
findings.detail:
When `dim1 == rank()-1 && dim2 == rank()-2 && dims are equal`, `transpose` swaps shape and strides into `t` and returns it without cloning, leaving `is_transposed_ = false`. For e.g. transpose(1,0) on `{n,n}` this yields strides `{1,n}`, which is not row-major — `is_contiguous()` on the result correctly returns false.

The comment immediately below states the invariant the rest of the codebase relies on: "Clone to contiguous: all math ops assume flat data()[i] indexing". That invariant is broken by the early return. Every kernel, `clone`, `copy_from`, `fill`, `serialize` and `AutogradEngine::matmul_op` (autograd_engine.cpp:43, `scalar_gemm_bt(a.data<float>(), b.data<float>(), ...)`) indexes `data()[i]` flat, so a fast-path transpose result is read in its untransposed memory order — silently wrong values, no crash.

No live caller currently hits the fast path (`transformer.cpp:320-322,491` and `autograd_engine.cpp:276` all transpose dims (1,2) of rank-4 tensors, where `dim1 != rank()-1`; `tests/test_tensor.cpp:112` uses (0,1) on rank-2, also not matching), so this is a latent trap in a public API. Related: the `Tensor(Shape, shared_ptr<Buffer>, DType)` constructor at line 73 never checks the buffer is large enough for `shape.numel()*dtype_size`, so a Tensor can legally claim more elements than its buffer holds.

find:tf-core.summary: Reviewed the core tensor/memory layer, the compute backends, and the SIMD kernels (C++20), reading the risky files in full rather than sampling. The tree is in better shape than the hotspot list suggests in some places — `block_codec.cpp`'s BitReader/FastBitReader and `gguf_bridge.cpp`'s offset validation are genuinely defensive, and `tensor_view.h` asserts contiguity where `tensor.cpp` does not — but three defects stand out as production-breaking. First, `kernel_gemm.cpp`'s `avx2_gemm` and `avx2_tiled_gemm` load B contiguously along its row instead of with stride N, so they fold N into the dot product and return the wrong matrix product for any N>1; this is wired into `CPUAVX2Backend::gemm`, the advertised CPU AVX2 backend, and diverges from the scalar reference in the same file. Second, the hand-rolled Vulkan ABI mirror declares `VkPhysicalDeviceMemoryProperties.memoryTypes` fields in the opposite order to the real driver struct (`heapIndex` before `propertyFlags`), so every memory-type query — `find_memory_type` on both Vulkan backends and `has_unified_memory` on the iGPU path — reads the heap index as if it were the property mask; that silently disables integrated-GPU zero-copy on hardware that supports it and can lead to `vkMapMemory` on non-host-visible memory. Third, the autograd registry is guarded by two different mutexes, with the `~Tensor` destructor hook taking `param_mutex_` while register/backward/clear take `mutex_`, leaving `param_map_` mutated concurrently. Below those, the theme is unchecked shape math: `Tensor::copy_from` validates numel but never dtype (memcpy length taken from the destination, so mismatched dtypes overflow the heap), `slice`/`transpose` accept negative dims and `start>end` (negative extents wrap `size_bytes()` to a huge size_t), contiguity is computed but never consulted so dim-1 tensor-parallel shards are read as flat buffers, and `CPUAVX2Backend::gemm` never checks that C can hold M*N. The two AVX2 quant GEMVs in `kernel_production.cpp` (quant4 overreads x by 16 bytes and double-counts; quant8 pairs 7 of 8 gather groups with the wrong activations) are real but currently have no in-tree callers — as do `Tensor::transpose`'s no-clone fast path, the `MemoryPool(0)` nullptr-deref, and the `TensorParallel*` subsystem — so I have ranked them accordingly. No tests exercise any AVX2 kernel path; the suite runs the scalar references, which is why the quant8/quant4/gemm divergences have gone unnoticed. Net: the scalar and reference paths look sound and well-hardened, but every runtime-dispatched SIMD and hand-rolled-ABI path needs a correctness test against its scalar twin before it can be trusted.
